extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom editors, media watchdogs, and readers interested in journalism ethics
extracted.subtask_description: An analytical piece outlining ethical standards, failures, and best practices around conflicts of interest in journalism, focused on newsroom responsibilities, disclosure, corrections, and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The Society of Professional Journalists—and most newsrooms—have codes of ethics that instruct journalists, in the first place, to avoid conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure is framed as a last resort; reporters should not have financial relationships with the subjects they cover. Example antipatterns: columnists writing about organizations that financially support their outside work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure is a last resort and must be meaningful
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure should be used only if conflicts are absolutely unavoidable: 'Disclosure is a last resort, if conflicts are absolutely unavoidable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belated disclosures (adding notes after publication) are insufficient if used inconsistently or without transparency about scope; disclosures should clearly state the nature of ties so readers can assess potential bias. Example: the Times appended belated financial disclosures to some columns after outside reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors must actively enforce ethical rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Undisclosed conflicts in journalism seem to be less a problem of unethical reporters, and more a problem of newsrooms not enforcing ethical rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should not merely accept reporters' clearances at face value; they must proactively police conflicts, respond to complaints, and apply policies consistently. Antipattern: editors overlooking conflicts among columnists or failing to respond to concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not write about entities that pay you or that you solicit funds from
rubrics_metrics.description: You just can’t write about people that you take money from. Certainly not people that you’re trying to go out and solicit money from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a journalist has been paid by or is actively soliciting funds from an organization, they should recuse themselves from coverage of that organization. Example: concerns about a columnist funded by Gates writing about Gates-funded projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recusal or resignation from external paid roles when incompatible
rubrics_metrics.description: When paid outside engagements create incompatible conflicts, journalists should resign or recuse themselves (example: David Brooks resigned his paid position with the Aspen Institute after it was deemed incompatible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations should require journalists to avoid outside roles that present obvious conflicts, and to step down from such roles when conflicts affect their reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full transparency in bios and disclosure statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Author bios and disclosures should clearly state the nature and scope of outside work and clients so readers can weigh potential bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a full list of corporate clients and explicit descriptions of roles (e.g., consultant, fundraiser) rather than vague titles. Example problem: a bio that lists a title without making clear what the author actually does, hindering readers' ability to assess bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue timely corrections or updates when undisclosed conflicts are revealed
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations should correct the record or add disclosures to previously published work when undisclosed conflicts are discovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrections should be comprehensive, transparent, and applied consistently across affected items. Antipattern: selective belated disclosures that leave many related columns uncorrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use journalistic or editorial voice to promote entities you have financial ties to
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should not leverage editorial content to promote entities to which they have financial ties (example: William Laurence using the Times’s editorial voice to promote a science exhibit while taking outside pay).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid favorable coverage or advocacy for projects, products, or events that financially benefit the journalist or their outside employers/clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vet sources and avoid quoting non-independent experts as independent
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must ensure quoted experts are truly independent and not undisclosed associates (example: a journalist quoting her literary agent as an independent expert led to removal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for relationships between sources and the journalist; if a source has a relevant relationship, disclose it or avoid using them as an independent expert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish and publicize clear, consistent processes for corrections and disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms should have transparent processes explaining how they decide which past items need disclosures or corrections and should communicate that process publicly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antipattern: refusing to explain why some columns received disclosures while others did not. Consistency and openness about technical or editorial hurdles is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid normalization of conflicts across journalistic institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The increasing normalization of conflicts (e.g., industry-sponsored seminars, university partnerships with corporations) undermines journalism’s ability to interrogate conflicts on beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions like journalism schools, conferences, and centers should avoid accepting funding that creates compromising relationships or at least be transparent and manage such conflicts robustly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proactively respond to watchdog and public concerns rather than waiting for outside exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms should not rely on outside investigators to surface ethical oversights; internal oversight should catch conflicts before they require public embarrassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build internal review, respond promptly to credible concerns raised by readers or watchdogs, and take remedial action without waiting for external pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about co-authoring projects with subjects you cover
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-authoring a book or project with a subject of coverage (example: a reporter co-authoring with Michael Phelps while covering him) creates an obvious conflict and can warrant suspension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid such collaborations while covering the subject; disclose and recuse if prior commitments exist and cannot be unwound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide adequate disclosure of the nature (not just existence) of ties
rubrics_metrics.description: Where disclosures are made, they should specify the exact nature of the relationship (e.g., paid work, board membership, fundraising) rather than ambiguous mentions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specificity allows readers to better assess potential bias; vague labels or silence about details obstruct transparency (example: refusals to provide a full list of corporate clients).
